question: Frontex recently published its January 2024 report on illegal entries by immigrants into the EU and noted a sharp rise in entries via the Western Africa route. Illegal immigrants who take that route arrive in the Canary Islands (Spain). It is surprising to see a leap in the numbers recorded: a 48% rise in illegal crossings on the December 2023 figures.
The Canary Islands have become the main gateway for illegal immigrants to Europe without Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist Government having protected Spain’s and the EU’s external borders properly. 1.
What view does the Commission take of that spike?

Given that Frontex recognises that the Canary Islands are the main illegal immigration access route into Europe, what specific steps will the Commission take to stop illegal entries and mitigate the negative effects of the arrival of thousands of illegal immigrants into the Canary Islands?

With a view to making dangerous boat journeys unattractive, is the Commission considering entering into negotiations with Mauritania and/or Senegal to establish a regional disembarkation platform similar to the one negotiated between Italy and Albania?
answer: To reduce irregular migration towards the EU in the Atlantic, the Commission is progressing in the implementation of the action plan for the Western Mediterranean and Atlantic routes, in particular as regards strengthening cooperation with partner countries along the migratory route and initiatives aiming at fighting irregular migration and creating alternative legal pathways.

On 8 February 2024, the President of the Commission met with President Ghazouani to reinforce the EU-Mauritania partnership and on 7 March 2024, Commissioner for Home Affairs signed a migration partnership with Mauritania. Upon the request of Spain, the Commission is providing support to the Canary Islands to address the consequences of the peak of arrivals.

In addition to the support provided by the European Border and Coast Guard Agency and the EU Agency for Asylum, Spain has at its disposal funding from the EU budget implemented through programmes under the Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs’ Funds.
Furthermore, the Commission is currently assessing a request by Spain for emergency assistance funding to support measures addressing the irregular migration towards the Canary Islands.

Furthermore, the Commission considers that the rise of irregular migration to the Canary Islands during this winter confirms that it is of utmost importance to that all Member States swiftly adopt and implement all the instruments under the Pact for Migration and Asylum (1) necessary for a comprehensive approach to managing migration effectively and fairly.
